blocks.x: We're going to start it. We can start off any time you're ready and you can just give your name again so we'll have your name on here if we know who to identify it. Yeah. Just give your name. What is your full name, Mr. Albert? Thomas Albert. Thomas Albert. Any middle name or initial? No, it's called Thomas Albert. Can you tell us just when you were born? Where were you born and just when was it?
I was born in, I was born in Alligate. I was born in 1877, the 23rd day of December. You're 80, it'll soon be 82 years over. Yeah, the 23rd of December will be 82.
You made it before Christmas. Yeah. What was the first instrument you took up as you started on violin or trumpet?

Guitar. Guitar, the first instrument. Did you have any lessons on it or just pick it up? No, just picked it up. And violin, I take lessons. You took lessons on that? Yeah, I take lessons from the old professor from the French Opry. Jimmy Fallow, he died. He was taking lessons. And when he takes his lesson that evening, I'll go to him and take lessons from him.
And he'll give you the same lesson then? Same lesson, yeah.

Remember you told me that before, right? Yeah. And so… Went right through the same book then as he did. Yeah. Well, then before I take up my violin, I take the lesson for about six months. Division. Division. Oh, just counting the time? Just counting the time, Division, yeah. And did you have to sing along with the music to learn that? No. No. Just like, Do Re Mi For Soul, I Say Do. Yeah. That's all right. Yeah. You see, I was being silent. Do Re Mi For Soul, I Say Do. Just counting it out with my hand. Just counting it out with my hand. Like the conductor of an artist. Yeah. Yeah. Now, you see, these days, one, two, and three, one, two, and three, but I didn't… No, you like that. Do Re Mi For Soul, I Say Do.
Well, let me see, I had one down, one to the right, one back to the left, and then…

That's right. Do Re Mi For Soul, see? It's a… you know, in your method, it's got the… Little arrows. And arrows. Yes, I've seen those. You see them? Yes, I've seen them. The ABC book, they used to have one dollar. You can't get them no more.
That was the method you used?
Yeah, one dollar. And it was a book like that. Oh, yeah. Yeah. And I used to, you know, one, two, one, two, one, two. You see? Yes. One, two, three. One, two, three. Yes. Wall side, one, two, three.
Yes. I'm wondering, did you pat your foot with that or just use your hand?

Well, after I knowed with my hand, I used my feet. See? One, two, three. One, two, three. You see? Same thing with your foot, man. One, two, three, four. One, two, three, four. See? One, two, one, two, three. One, two, three. One, two, three. And you used your foot in the same direction. Oh, yeah. Yeah. You see? Just like you would the baton when you direct an orchestra. Yeah. The same thing. You see?
And you did that for six months before you took up the violin.

Yeah, before I took up the violin. Then I take the violin. But the cornet, I didn't take it. I know the music. Yeah. All I had to do, by a method. And, uh, at the, uh, fainting, you understand? Get the tone, A, B, you know, after I got the tone, I know the music, that's all. I just wanted to know the scales. Yeah. Right. So about how old were you when you started on, uh, guitar? When I was about, uh, I was about 17 years old.
17. Yeah. And then, uh, how late did you start on the violin? How much later did you start on the violin?

Well, afterwards, uh, the guitar was too slow. And I went and got the violin. So I left the band for about, oh, about six or seven years. And then, uh, it got a little too slow. So I went and bought a cornet.
Yeah. Did you play guitar in the band then too, when you took that violin?
Well, I could play it, but I never did, uh, uh, I hired somebody else. Just after I took the violin. Yeah. Uh, it was the lead, you see.
I mean, when you started on guitar, were you playing with other people or did I play yourself?
No, no. I was by myself.
By yourself.
Yeah. I played by myself.
How long did you play violin before you got in a band then?

Well, after I got the band, I, well, about, uh, well, let me see. You see how long I played violin? I played violin about, uh, about a year, I believe it was a year after I got the, uh, ruled upon the music. Then I, uh, know the music. Then I just picked up the violin and, and, and Jimmy, uh, my teacher was showing me the ferns and everything. And then afterwards I bought music from Little Feast.
Oh, yes.
From New York. I joined that, uh, club.
Oh, yes. Where they send you the orchestration.
Yes. Every year, every month I get, uh, two copies. Uh-huh. You don't do that to work with it.
No, they don't do that at all. You have to buy them all.
Yeah.
Great.
Yeah.
Um, what was the first band you played with? What was the name of it? Do you remember?
Well, uh, it was your own band or? Yeah, it was my old Tom Albersman. Yeah, they called me Tom Albersman, yeah.
I wonder, uh, Tom, uh, got a card that first came.
Yeah, Ralph, uh, Ralph got this card, an old card of yours from, uh, Professor Mineta. Yeah. It has a picture of a short carnet on it.

Yeah, it has a kind of carnet. And I wonder, it says, Kid Albert's Jazz Band. Kid Albert, yeah. Well, yeah. Let's see, where were you living then? That was on, um... Uh, 28th, what's that? 2610? Uptown, 8th Street.
8th Street.
Oh, yeah.
2610 8th Street then. Yeah. Uptown, number there.
Yeah. Well, that was the...
So when was that about? Do you know?

Oh, now, partner. Was that before the First World War, after the war? Kid Albert, and Kid Albert Band. Music, funny for occasion, yeah. Tom Albert, you see? Tom Albert, they called me Tom Albert, but he...and Thomas Albert too, you see that? Yeah.
They also called him Kid Albert.
Yeah, well, when I was in the band, I was called Kid Albert. Kid Albert.
You'd be blowing trumpet then.
I was blowing trumpet.
Oh, yeah. Really a carnet, I guess.

Yeah, one of these. Yeah, yeah. A little sharp carnet. Yeah, the first carnet I bought, over here on, uh, right from here, uh, let me see, you don't know, uh, what street that, uh, what that furniture place right in front of you? Oh, yeah, I know. It, it, it had a ice house. Yeah, where that ice house is. You see, right? Let me see, you don't know, uh...
See, Grimwald was down there once on Charter Street, years ago. That was way back though.

No, you was on, uh, I'll tell you what it was, the first, a book I bought for the carnet, and the first trumpet, I bought it from old man, used to have a music store on, uh, Royal, on Charter Street. Charter, between, uh, they had a music store between, uh, St. Louis and Courtei.
Up down there.
Right by the, uh, had an ice house. Yeah.
Where the courthouse is now, maybe?
No, the courthouse. On the other side. No, the courthouse is the next corner. See, the courthouse, in this block. No, the courthouse was in the next block. Yeah. You mean the old courthouse?
No, it's the new courthouse now.

Oh, the new courthouse now, that was, uh, oh yes, it's in that block. It's in that block, yeah. Yeah, well that's the new courthouse, what they got there now? Yeah. What they building there now? No, I'm talking about that, the corner. No, it's a hotel. That's a hotel. Uh-huh. Yeah, it's right in that block. Yeah. Yeah, it's right in that block. You had a, uh, old man there selling all kinds of, uh, uh, instruments, any kind of piece of music, riders, lances. Did you get your carnet? Yeah, yeah, I bought the corner, it had a snake on it. A little snake on it. It had a snake. A little snake on it. A corner at the lake, that's where it had a snake on it. Oh, yeah. Yeah.
So when would that be, Tim?
Oh, finally, that's been there, Lord.
That'd be before the First World War, right? Yes, yes.
Yes.
You must have had your carnet when you played with Fess, didn't you, in that first band that Fess was in? Yes.
Fess, yes.
Because he said he played, sometime he'd play carnet and then...
Then I played violin.
And then when you'd get the heart, his lip would give out.

Then I played violin, yeah. Great. Oh, Jesus, that's been, uh, oof. That's the first time I've carried him down in the country on a cane farm. You know, in the cane cart in the morning. When a big cart, he told me about that once. Yeah, had three mules in that.
What do you call it, the cane cart?

Yeah, the whole cane in it. Yeah, yeah. And they come to get us, uh, the carnet down there, we finished grinding, you know. Just giving a little dance down there for the people. And the Fess, and, uh, I believe I carried a, uh, uh, uh, um, that fella insurance man, there, his cousin.
Oh, uh, Humphrey, uh... Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Jules Lee was the, wait, Jules Barnes.
Jules Barnes used the trombone.
The trombone, and Lee was the drummer.
It was the drummer, yeah.
I was going to ask one thing about this card. It says Kid Albert's Jazz Band. When did they start using the word jazz for the bands?
Well, we always did use that word, jazz band. Kid Albert's Jazz Band.
I mean, in the real old days, did they call it jazz or ragtime bands?
Well, they called it jazz and ragtime. They called it both.
How early do you remember they using that word jazz? Did they use it, like when you played with Fest, do you remember way back there? Did they ever call it jazz then or just ragtime?

Jazz band, yeah. Used to call it jazz band. I always did know we called it jazz band. Ragtime band, we never heard that, but jazz band. That's what we used in my time. But they didn't have no drums then. And they didn't have no sliding trombone. That's been quite a while for. Yeah. Yeah.
Was there such a thing as a ragtime band though in those days? Well, they used that word too, ragtime.
They used that word too. They used that word too. They used that word too. They used that jazz and ragtime. Yeah. Was there any difference between the two styles that you thought of?
No, it wasn't the same thing. Yeah, it was the same thing.

Dragtime and jazz was the same thing, but they used that word. Yeah. But the moistery used to your jazz. Yeah. That's the moistery used to your jazz thing. I was going to ask a little bit about the brass bands you were just talking about. You played with the Henry Allen band. Henry Allen, yeah.
And the Eureka.
Eureka. Yeah. Were you one of the first members of the Eureka?
Do you remember when they started that? No. It was, I was playing with Allen. Eureka was playing then. One of the men's died and died.
In the Eureka. So they took me to rehearsal with them.
I went to rehearsal with them and played first. Eureka. Eureka. Were you one of the first members of the Eureka? Do you remember when they started that?

No. I was playing with Alan. Eureka was playing then. But one of the men's died, I think, in the Eureka. So they take me to rehearsal with them. I went there and rehearsed with them and I played twice. Twice the trumpet.
Do you remember some of the other fellas that were in the Eureka when you...
John Kazmi. He was in the Eureka. There was Jimmy.
Jimmy was that the drummer?

The drummer. Jimmy, they had a big fella, he died. He was playing a funeral across the road there. He used to play the tour. He died. He got sick and died. I believe he died on the way. I think he did. He told me it was coming from one of the other sides of Gretchen. Yeah. I never knew it.
It wasn't Eddie Jackson. No, it wasn't Eddie Jackson.
You don't use these, do you? No, I think about it.
There was Red Clark in the band when you were there. Who? Red Clark, Joseph Clark. He played trombone. He played trombone one time.
Connish. I know Connish was playing trombone. And Connish was playing trombone. And they had another fella play trombone with Connish. But he died.
Yes.
I just forgot his name. But he died. And then we got Warner. Oh, yes. After they got Warner. And then Connish died and we got Red.
Oh, yes. I see.
And after they got Red, and Willie, Johnny, Willie died. Willie died first. That's the leader.
Yes.

And Johnny's brother, he was playing the baritone. He died afterwards. And then Connish, he died. Well, most of them, most of them, most of them, yes. And there were fellas playing alto, he died. Yeah, a fella played alto, I call him Buddy. He used to, the name Buddy, he used to work at the, at the, this, this clothing place right there, right on Connell Street there. What's he called? A clothing place? Yeah, he used to work, he used to work there. Oh, oh, wow. What'd you call that? Big clothing store. Yeah, on that side, on Connell Street. I don't know, there's Stine.
Joyce. Oh, Joyce, I don't know.
Yeah, yeah. Well, he didn't name Buddy, he used to play alto.
Did they have any saxophones in the band then?

They didn't have no saxophones in the band then. We were using clarinet. Who was the clarinet player? John Cassidy. Oh, that's right, you told us. Yeah. And then afterwards, we started to use in the sax. Yeah. And the fellow we started using sax with, he's up there in town, he's a barber uptown there now. He started to say, I don't know, forgot his name. A barber uptown?
Yeah.
Yeah.
I guess a lot of musicians from barbers, they said. Yeah.
We'd never know it.
Anyway, that's quite a few of the names. I wondered about Henry Allen's band. Who else was in that? You played the carnet with Henry Allen. Yeah.
I played the carnet.
Was there another carnet too?
Henry, me, Henry, and we used to use sometimes Kimball sometimes. And then used to use John Peloton. Oh yeah. Use him sometimes. And sometimes we'd use Georgie Hooker.
Oh yeah, I've heard of it all.
Yeah, we used him sometimes. We just, you know, what we don't have. We don't have a use. You know.
Who were the trombones over there?

Buddy. Buddy Johnson. Buddy Johnson. Buddy Johnson. Buddy Johnson and the, what's this other trombone, and Eddie Vincent, he learned with me. Me and him learned together. And he started playing trombone with me. Excelsior. Yeah. Yeah. Well he started playing trombone.
Did you play, was the, who was the Excelsior band? Well I never did play with Excelsior.
You didn't play? I never did.
Who was the leader of that?

Joe, Joe, Joe Lizard. Joe Lizard. He was the leader of the Excelsior band. Yeah, I know the band, but they used to wear green suits. What kind of suits did Henry Allen's band wear? Well we used to wear, we used to have them kind of a, we used to wear white pants and blue pants, you know, all white atlas we played. Then we, for funeral, we'll have a blue, no we'd have a blue blouse and white. You understand? For funeral we'll have a black shirt and blue pants. Oh, I see. Yeah, you look darker color.
Dark color, yeah. Yeah.

And then for, and for red like that we'll have a blue blouse and white pants. White pants, yeah. Yeah. And you wore a cap? Yeah, a cap, yeah. The name on the cap. I got the name somewhere around here now. The cap if I didn't give it away, I'll give it away, the cap. With someone from the Spade of Eureka, the initials and everything. Yeah. It'd be nice to have that old hat, the big cap.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. $3 for a funeral and most you could get is $5 for a parade. Now like on the place for the bulls, not the bulls to El Noro, but we paid us $10.
Is that for carnival? That's carnival. Yeah.

Paid us $10 a man. For all day long? That's all day long from 6 to 6. Yeah, from 6 to 6. 6 in the morning? 6 to 6. We go up there all in the morning and bring them all around to pick up the gang. And then we start up. What do you mean? You're tired after that? Oh man, you're tired. I guess you're tired. Then walk up there and—no, we walk coming this way, then we walk back. That's two trips. That's about 60 some odd blocks, ain't it? Oh yeah, the time they go all around? Yeah. Way up on the other side of the park. Yeah, on the other side of the park. Yeah. Audubon Park. Yeah. Yeah. Oh man, that was terrible. I stayed there for three, uh, four seasons. Yeah, but it was time. When you finish there, you've got enough. Then I leave there, and the truck be waiting for me to go down to the islands some ways. I come here in these little boy, jump over the truck, go to the islands, say, go down to Shell Beach, go down to Muzzle the River. Muzzle the River. Muzzle the River. islands away. I come here in these little boys, jump over the truck, go to the island, say, go down to Shell Beach, go down to Mouth of the River, go down to Boyle Woods. We used to catch that train here in Allogies. They call it the Shell Beach. Shell Beach train. Yes. No, this is Shell Beach over here, the Grand Island. That's a train in Allogies. Before they broke it up, you understand, we used to have coaches. We used to catch it to the Burris. As we go to Burris, we catch a mail boat. Oh, go by boat for a while. Yeah, we go to Burris. After we get to Burris, we play a tune and we catch the mail boat and we get on hit there about six o'clock in the evening. Now it looked like it's almost as far from Burris as here. Burris here. Yeah, on the mail boat. Was that the Grand Isle? That's the Grand Isle. That's the Grand Isle. Yeah. We used to go down there and play. Boyle Woods, Farley Town, that's when the ships be coming in from the Gulf. See, the ships be coming in from the Gulf. We'd be on the wharf there. We'd be on the ship. We'd be on the ship. We'd be on the ship.

Well, listen, Tom, when you were playing those long parades like that and you got towards the end, you were getting tired, did you play music a little easier for you to play or did you just keep playing the, I mean, did you have tunes that you thought were a little easier?

Easy? A little easier? Yes. Sometimes you get tired and you pick up a little anything which you think is easy. Yeah. So there's hard marches where we play them when we first start. Yeah, that's right. Yeah, there's hard marches. You see we play them, sometimes you get some tough pieces of march sometimes. But we play them when we first, we refresh. Yeah. Yeah. And when we're coming back, we pick up a little anything.
Yeah. Yeah. One little tune here, I had a note that Fess was telling once that you played, if you don't shake, you don't get no cake. Don't get no cake. Yeah.
Is that one of your favorite numbers? Yeah. You don't shake, you don't get no cake.
Can you remember how that went? Yeah. Let me see.

Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm Do you know who wrote that or what was that? I don't know, we just picked it up from the other bands yesterday. A fellow who'd make that up, you see a fellow who'd make that up, little than anything. You make it up and you make a hit out of it. But all the music we'd get it from, you used to call me a parlor, a parlor musician.
Oh I see, what did that mean?

You see I wasn't a head man so much. I see. You understand? I see the music, now if I see the music I play with it about two or three times, well I'd get the chorus. Then I'd have it. Then I'd have it. With the voice I couldn't get it, you understand? As long as I get it, play it two or three times and get that chorus then I'd start on it. But you had to see the music, you see. But some fellows would hear the singing again, but I'd rather play by the music.
What'd they call that again?

A parlor. They called me a parlor. They used to call me a parlor music. But after a while all of them would come by the parlor music. Yeah. Yeah, a musician. They used to call me a parlor musician because I used to play all the music, you understand? And like the piano and the thing, you put the coffee up there and play it. You see, that one used to call me a parlor musician. Yeah. But when they come to parlor, when they had to read, they all of them come to me. Every one of them, every one of them come to me. For the light of this, the light of that. Sam Morgan, all of them little bands, Rene, Chris Kelly, all of them little bands, all of them little bands, all of them little bands come to me. But still they used to call me a parlor, a parlor musician. But when they find out, they was getting them tuned so fast, you understand? They couldn't think of them. Then they come to me and want a light. Yeah. Yeah. Some of them would know the music. Some of them know the music just as good, but they didn't know the division. Yeah, they didn't know the division. See, the division is the principal part.
It's by the… Yeah. The music. The count of the lives.

The division. If you know the lives, you can't play. Some of them know the music though. They get up there, they play, they play, but when you come to a club, you play with somebody else you don't know why you're at. It's just as bad. Well I tried to show them. Johnny Lindsay, he was playing with the rubber shows. He's in the, Johnny Lindsay plays trombone. And he was playing at the larynx thing. And I was living right there at that chord. See that chord you've got there, five or twelve dolphins. Oh yeah, yeah. Johnny Lindsay, when they play at night, then they get off for lunch, you know, and go back to play for that matinee in the evening. He'd come and he took two, three lessons. With me at five or twelve dolphins in the street.
Three lessons.
Johnny Lindsay, he's playing when he could play. He played trombone. He used to play bass.
I heard him on bass.

Yeah. And so first night I brought him in the final room, then I had a little music and we played together. He played. But he wasn't sure. He could play to me but he wasn't sure. So he played and I had a piece of music from Liofice. It was the walls. And I think it was in three flats. And we used using that long shank. Is that what?
Long shank.
You see they had two shanks there. Put it in the key of A or something. Put the key in there, change key.
On your cornet.

On the cornet. Oh, I see. You used to have a long shank that puts you in A and then you take that off, put the other shank on and puts you in B. Oh, I see, yeah. You see? And I took that shank off and I put it in A and I said if you could play this, I said you can go to myself. And so I started a brand new piece. I just come from Liofice. I had two pieces coming. I said this is tough old. It's about five shops I think it was. Five flats for him and shops for me. And he played, he played, he played, he played, he played, he played, he played, he played, he played, he played, he played, he played, he played, he played, he played. He played again and I said no last time.
I said let's play this again.

And he played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played and I played It has been many years. Been many years. It's been almost about thirty-five years.
He died about eight years ago.
He died. In Chicago. Yes, and I haven't saw him since. He went up to stay in Chicago. He took three lessons with me. And I told him he could go, but he could play. He knows it. But he wasn't sure.
Did his father read music, do you think?
No, no, no.
Or his brother heard music?

His brother, no. No, I played with them too. He had a little fellow playing with him. Joe, what did they have? Joe, we called him Joe. A little bit of a little fellow playing cornet with him. So I went round there and... Jack Fajida. He used to play with the old man, Johnny. Johnny was playing bass. Herbert was playing violin. The old man was playing guitar. Jack Fajida. Jack Fajida. Jack Fajida. He was playing a little bit of a little bit of a... Cornet. Cornet. Yeah, he didn't have no crannets. Let's see. Who was playing, he didn't have no crannets on the blade. They ought to have a lead there.
Oh yeah. Who was playing violin. Oh yeah, so that was a lead. Yeah, it was a lead.
And so I was there and I played, I took his place. And so Sam Morgan, he was playing in the hall across the river there. He stole the...
Isaiah. Let me see how that thing was.
Let me see how that thing was.
It's always there that I played. I took his place.

And so Sam Morgan, he was playing in the hall across the river there. And Sam Morgan, he stole the Isaiah. Let me see how that thing was. I believe it was Sam. Sam Morgan, Jack Paeda was playing trumpet in the band across there and Sam Morgan, he went over there. He got sick. Jack Paeda got sick. Sam Morgan, he went over there in his place and hid him over his face. So when he got better they find him. And that's why he made the band up, Sam Morgan's band. Yeah, and I was the first one to start him to cross the lake.
Yeah.

I started him to cross the lake. Sometimes I played two trumpet. I carried two trumpet. You know, they helped me out sometimes. Couldn't get no piano. I played two trumpet. Well, the piano said, well, I take two trumpet. Sometimes no trombones. I said, well, I was the first one. And then they got big. Mo Beers, then he was Morgan's band, was a nice band then. I was the first one to cross then. Well, I used to play everywhere. All around Hmong City. All around from to Bonmore. Bonmore. We got off in Lafayette, Bonmore. And the place from Bonmore, they called it to, where the refound rat. Is that up the river? No, it's down on the coast.
No, that's where, that's where in Texas. Oh, that's in Texas. That's in Texas.
I was going to ask you, Fort Arthur, is it that far over there? Oh, yeah, that's in Texas. After you hit the line of Orange, Texas, hit the line of Orange, Texas, then you hit Beaumont. Beaumont.
Beaumont.

Yeah. Oh, I see. And hit Beaumont, Fort Arthur. Now you have to get to Beaumont, where we have a hotel in Beaumont, where we played that night. Then they had another little train come from Beaumont and carry you to Fort Arthur. Thirty-five cents. Where we go to Beaumont and we play that night. And then we'll come back and play in the, I don't know, one more, and then Fort Arthur one night. You understand? Four four.

I'm, I'm, I'm not going to cut you off, but when you were, when you were just young in the music, just starting in the music, can you remember any of the other bands they had around here? Press talks about the, uh, Bollin.
Bollin, Bollin, Bollin, yes. Oh yes, Bollin band, well that was, that was about the best band most, them times. In them times. And then the, the trumpet. How did Bollin play?
Did you hear him play?

Oh yeah, oh yeah, it was ragtime, that was ragtime, ragtime, ragtime, you know, all them blues and everything like that. Loud, you could hear him. Four o'clock in the morning, you could hear him cross the road. Yeah, yeah. It was just loud, you know, playing like, didn't care, you know. Just didn't care? Didn't care, you know, them fellas. He just hit the notes all right.
He just hit the notes. Oh yeah.

Yeah, I never did see him read a piece of music though. Well, one time I went to see him play at the, at the old fellas hall, and I sit down there, and I sit down there, I sit down there, and the first time I went in there, looking at him and Carnish, and Buddy, Bollin, and Bob Lyons, all of the players. I sit down there, but I must be having my mouth open. And sitting down there, you know, I had my mouth open looking at them playing. But after I got up from playing, I must have had dust in here. I did like that, man, I couldn't hardly have to swallow all that dust. Then that was my mouth open looking at them.
Oh yeah, you've been just so interested.

Yeah. I sit down there looking at them, the first time I'd been close to him playing, you understand. I sit down there, and I was a lad, just start the playing. And I just sat there, I must be with my mouth open, and I must have swallowed all that dust. Yeah, it does smell like dust. Yeah, you know. And I did like that. You didn't get your breath. You did. I must have swallowed some dust down there. And so they went, afterwards they went crazy, you know. Did he play anything like your band playing? Who?
Did Golden, did he play in a similar style to your band, or?

Well, yes, they all played the same thing, like you don't shake, you don't get no kick, you know, such a thing. They used to play all that. All that stuff, we'll hear that fella play. We'll play, we'll catch and play, we'll catch our band, we'll play it you see. And we'll see the other fella playing something good, right? Right, right, we'll catch it and we'll play it. You catch it from one another, you understand.
Did they have a nice beat for the band, they keep a good time? Anything special about that band?

No, all you got to do, when you're going to stop, you see when you're going to start, you see I was a leader, that's me getting ready. Oh yeah. Let's get ready, all right. One stop. That's one, that's to get ready. All of them didn't got up, got this in. Ah ha. Let's stop, I had my mind, he's in my corner, and I'll play. Oh yeah. One, two, three on the fourth.
Yeah, one, two, three.
On the fourth one you start, right? Yeah, one, two, three, and I'll go. Now when we're going to stop? Oh, wait a minute.
One beat, and when would you get that, when you start the last chorus or?
Yeah, when we're going to stop, one beat.
How soon would you give them warning you're going to stop? During the last chorus or the beginning of the last chorus or what?

Beginning of the last chorus, yeah, I don't care if we start, if we get on the chorus, you say, well we're going to stop in that chorus. Sometimes we play a chorus and we're going to play it again. If we don't play it, play it with one start, we'd stop.
That means when you get to the end of that chorus, that's it?
Yes, that's it, yeah. Right. Once, once, it wants to get ready. Three to start, and one to stop.
All the bands used to do that?
All the bands, yeah, just come out just as even. I guess Buddy used to do that too, Buddy.
Oh yeah, yeah, sure. Would he be standing up or sitting down? Sitting down.
Sitting down. Yeah, sitting down, sitting down, he'd stand up, he'd just sit down. What did he never bother with music? Yeah, very some of you holler with music, sometimes, routine all the time.
Yeah.
Played the same kind of numbers over there?
Yeah, over and over, over and over.
Yeah, did he play many blues, do you remember?

Yeah, most all blues. Plenty of blues. Yeah, blues. Sometime about twelve o'clock, they'd play a quadrillion. After twelve o'clock, they'd play a charlots. Some of the halls. Some of the halls, you know, they don't want it. They can't dance it. With the white folks, we would play lances. See? That's what we'd play lances. Is that something like a quadrillion? That's something like a quadrillion. Just the same as a quadrillion. And we'd shot us some time. And then again we'd play varietas. The holiday dance statue. I don't know if you're that. Yeah, I've seen some of the music, but. Yeah, varietas. That's a long thing. You've got waltzes and everything, two, three, all kinds of times. Oh, I see. Mixing. Mixing, yeah. That's a varietas. And it takes a good one to play that you know, of course.
Did you ever play many blues in your band?
Oh, yeah, that's always blues. Yeah. All kinds of blues.
Did you sort of make blues up as you played them or do you have any certain?

Well, when I hear the fellas play, yeah, when I hear the fellas play, the fellas come hear us play, they sit down, they go around and they play the same thing we play. That's all. Now for me, I did that music from Leo Feast, well I'll have something new. Yeah, you'll have some new numbers. You see, I have them new numbers, they get around and catch that and you see them playing it. Yeah, yeah. You know, they ain't got no music, but you see them, some of them got a quick head. Yeah, yeah. And as long as one can lead it, that's all. As long as the leader can lead it, the other fellas are going to follow.
Yeah, they'll follow.

They'll follow, that's all. Those you lead, they're going to follow. They call me a father player. I need my music you know. I was the first of Cadet Love and the SP, when the Navy first come there. The first building they had there, they had a dance for the soldiers. And we played in there that night in Cadet Love. Cadet Love? Cadet Love. Oh yeah. Yeah, Cadet Love. Cadet Love. Cadet Love. Oh yeah. Yeah. Cadet Love. I wanted to ask some more about your very early life. Over in Algiers, just where were you living in Algiers? What part of, do you remember the street about? Yes. Cadet Love. Cadet Love. Oh yeah. Yeah. Cadet Love.
I was living in Soxer Lane.
I started playing, Sox's Lane, in the Navy. They got all that for the Navy now. Oh, now for the Navy. Yes. They didn't have no Navy there. Way down there.
Way down in Sox's Lane.
They had a lane, go all the way back almost about three miles away.
I wonder where some of the old halls were there that you played. Do you remember the Navy?
Well they didn't have no halls there. They had the halls all in Algiers. We used to have to go in Algiers. I've been to Algiers. Yeah, but the way they used to give picnics under the oak trees.
Oh, you had picnics now where you lived?

Under the oak trees, yeah. White picnics and colored picnics, they had on the oak trees, big oak trees. They used to have on the Sunday night, Sunday night, you know, they'd have big picnics there. Or they'd have big time there, the brass bands sometimes they played. You see, and I'll open the night, they'd have the brass bands. Now I'm in there, Dorsey, big father. He had a big, nice band in there. Peter, his father was playing guitar. Peter, yeah, his father was playing with Dorsey's band. And he used to have a band come at Sox's Lane and Louie Arts. Had a big flat foam on a Sunday. They'd come there and start up at four o'clock. Three until twelve.
Peter, was that the Dorsey that Fess told us about one time when they didn't give him anything to eat? They asked him something about cheese? Big Dorsey, yeah.
He used to play these, yeah. Big Dorsey. What was that story? Eh?
What was that story? Oh yeah, that's when Fess pulled that with another problem.

Yeah, one time Fess mentioned that to Dandy Lewis, was it, or somebody, and he was going to hit him. And he thought they were laughing at him, but they were laughing about this fellow Dorsey. Dorsey, yeah. One time they didn't give the band anything to eat a drink.
Dorsey. Do you remember hearing about that?
Was that any, did all the musicians know about that?
What was that? Well Fess was telling me, but I didn't understand that. No. I didn't know what that was.
I think that was something like the fellow that went for the fish and something like that. Something like that.

Yeah. Something funny happened there. Yeah, it would be something happened there with Dorsey then. Of course his father used to play ghetto. And Peter was young and Fess was young, a young minister. Yeah. But they had a fine band. Dorsey had a fine band. And all the good musicians, them the fellows used to play all the music. Two cornets, trombone, clarinet, violin. And finally they had a band. All those fellows you know, they knew music. But they had a band sometimes, ten pieces.
You didn't have drums?
Well, they had drums afterwards. Yeah, they had drums.
They had drums.
Yeah, well that was afterwards.
A little later.
Yeah, a little later. Yeah. And the banjos, they used to use a guitar.
Or a guitar, no banjo.

No banjo. No banjo. No banjo. Now, there's always one that started to use in banjo. Of course, as they found this was much louder. Take the head off and… Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
I'm going to ask about the Elmira Pleasure Ground. You mentioned the picnics you had down where you were living. Where was the Elmira Pleasure Ground?
Elmira, that was in Algiers.
Right up in Algiers.
In Algiers, the Elmira Pleasure Ground. That's in the back. It was in the back, uh, had a little fence all around Elmira.
Was it near the river or near where the SP station was?

Where was the SP station? Right in the back there. Of course I was back there peeping through the fence and listening at the band and I was peeping through the fence and the policeman come back there and he hit me up.
Did you run in the middle of the band?
Yeah, I was peeping through the band like that. I was peeping through the back, and bam!
What were you looking at?
I looked at the band, the people dancing today. Listening to the music. Yeah, listening to the music. You weren't hurting everybody. Yeah, Elmira Pleasure Ground.
You wouldn't remember what band that was in the world?
No, no, I wouldn't remember what band that was.
The people were dancing that?

Yeah, they were dancing that night. But that's been quite a while. It must have been quite a while. Yeah, that's been quite a while. I was kind of a young fellow then, you know what I mean? Just stood by me. Anyway, I hear a band, I would go listen at them, try to catch them. Yeah. The best thing I would grab it.
Yeah.

You see, when you're doing music, you can get any instrument on you want to scale. Is that right? Yeah. Any instrument knows you want to scale after you know that music now. Get the scale of your instrument, well you see, you ain't got nothing to worry about the
You know the time and the counting.
Yeah, you ain't got nothing to worry about.
